blocks.text:
Design a Traffic Signal Control System for a road intersection. The system manages the traffic lights for each direction of traffic, cycles them safely through Red, Yellow and Green, and coordinates with pedestrian crossing signals.

  • Actors: approaching vehicles, waiting pedestrians, an emergency dispatcher, city traffic engineers.
  • Scope: a single intersection with two perpendicular traffic directions (North-South and East-West), each with its own signal.
  • Goal: guarantee that opposing, conflicting directions are never both green at once, while supporting configurable timing and pedestrian crossing requests.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: two vehicles from conflicting directions must never both have a green light at the same time. Every other requirement is secondary to that safety guarantee.
blocks.content:
Design a Traffic Signal Control System for a road intersection. The system manages the traffic lights for each direction of traffic, cycles them safely through Red, Yellow and Green, and coordinates with pedestrian crossing signals.

  • Actors: approaching vehicles, waiting pedestrians, an emergency dispatcher, city traffic engineers.
  • Scope: a single intersection with two perpendicular traffic directions (North-South and East-West), each with its own signal.
  • Goal: guarantee that opposing, conflicting directions are never both green at once, while supporting configurable timing and pedestrian crossing requests.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: two vehicles from conflicting directions must never both have a green light at the same time. Every other requirement is secondary to that safety guarantee.

items: The system shall control traffic signals for at least two perpendicular directions at one intersection.
Each signal shall cycle through RED, GREEN and YELLOW in a safe, predictable order.
The system shall support configurable durations for each color, per intersection.
The system shall notify pedestrian crossing signals whenever a vehicle signal changes.
The system shall support an emergency override that forces a specific direction green for priority vehicles.
The system shall support a pedestrian crossing request that can shorten the current green phase.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: safety, reliability, extensibility and observability

items: Safety: the core invariant (never both directions green) must be structurally impossible to violate, not just tested for.
Reliability: the intersection must fail toward a safe state (e.g. flashing red) rather than an undefined one if a component fails.
Extensibility: new timing strategies (e.g. sensor-based adaptive timing) must be addable without changing TrafficSignal or IntersectionController.
Observability: every signal change must be visible to anything that has registered interest, without tight coupling to the signal itself.
Thread Safety: the scheduler thread and an emergency override request may act on the same signal concurrently and must not corrupt its state.
Is this system for a single intersection, or a network of intersections that need to coordinate (a "green wave")? Assume single intersection unless stated otherwise.
Do pedestrian signals need their own independent timing, or do they always mirror the vehicle signal they are attached to?
Should the system support more than two perpendicular directions (e.g. a five-way intersection)?
Is persistence required (does signal state need to survive a restart), or is this purely an in-memory control loop?
Are timing durations fixed at deployment, or can a traffic engineer change them at runtime?
Exactly one intersection with two perpendicular signal groups: North-South and East-West.
Pedestrian signals directly mirror their associated vehicle signal (RED vehicle light means WALK is safe).
Timing strategy is pluggable but fixed-duration timing is the default implementation for this design.
The scheduler advances phases on a fixed timer; sensor-based dynamic adjustment is discussed as a future extension, not implemented here.
No persistence layer is required for the core control loop; a database design is still covered separately for audit logging.

metadata.alt: The five core entities: TrafficSignal, SignalState, SignalTimingStrategy, SignalObserver and IntersectionController

items: SignalColor: the enum of possible light colors, RED, YELLOW, GREEN.
SignalState: represents the signal’s current color and knows what color comes next.
SignalTimingStrategy: decides how long each color should last.
SignalObserver: anything that needs to react whenever a signal’s color changes.
TrafficSignal: one physical signal for one direction, combining a state, a timing strategy, and a list of observers.
IntersectionController: owns the two perpendicular signals and drives the safe phase cycle between them.

metadata.alt: IntersectionController composes two TrafficSignal instances, each holding one state and one strategy

items: Composition: IntersectionController composes its two TrafficSignal instances, they cannot meaningfully exist independently of the controller that coordinates them.
Aggregation: TrafficSignal aggregates a SignalTimingStrategy, the same strategy instance can be shared across multiple signals.
Association: TrafficSignal is associated with zero or more SignalObserver instances, added and removed independently of the signal’s own lifecycle.
Realization: GreenState, YellowState and RedState each realize the SignalState interface; FixedTimingStrategy realizes SignalTimingStrategy; PedestrianSignal realizes SignalObserver.

metadata.alt: Full class diagram: SignalState, SignalTimingStrategy and SignalObserver interfaces, their implementations, and how TrafficSignal and IntersectionController tie them together

blocks.text: Notice the three interfaces at the top of the diagram, SignalState, SignalTimingStrategy and SignalObserver. Every one of the design’s extension points is one of these three interfaces, this is deliberate, and is what section 9 covers in depth.
This design leans on three classic patterns, each solving a distinct problem the intersection actually has.

metadata.alt: The three signal states cycling Green to Yellow to Red and back to Green

blocks.text: Why needed: a signal’s current color determines both what it does and what it transitions to next, without the State pattern, this logic collapses into if-else chains checking an enum everywhere the color matters. Why best: each state class owns exactly its own transition rule, adding a new state (e.g. a flashing amber state for maintenance mode) means adding one new class, not touching existing ones. What it solves: keeps transition logic local to each state instead of scattered across the codebase.

metadata.alt: TrafficSignal depending on the SignalTimingStrategy interface, with FixedTimingStrategy and a future adaptive strategy both fitting behind it

blocks.text: Why needed: different intersections need different timing rules, a busy highway crossing needs longer green phases than a quiet residential corner, and some intersections may eventually use live sensor data. Why best: TrafficSignal never needs to change when a new timing approach is introduced, it only ever calls getDurationSeconds(color). What it solves: decouples "how long should this color last" from the signal itself.

metadata.alt: TrafficSignal notifying every registered observer, including PedestrianSignal and a monitoring dashboard, whenever its color changes

blocks.text: Why needed: pedestrian signals, monitoring dashboards, and potentially connected-vehicle notifications all need to react the instant a signal changes, without TrafficSignal needing to know any of them exist. Why best: new observer types can be added (a dashboard, a logging service) without ever touching TrafficSignal’s own code. What it solves: keeps TrafficSignal focused purely on its own state, while still supporting an open-ended set of interested listeners.

items: TrafficSignal: responsibility is managing one signal’s current state, its timing, and its observers. Attributes: id, state, timingStrategy, observers. Methods: advance(), forceState(), getCurrentColor(), getCurrentDurationSeconds().
IntersectionController: responsibility is coordinating exactly two signals so they never conflict. Attributes: northSouthSignal, eastWestSignal, phase. Methods: step(), applyPhase() (private).
GreenState / YellowState / RedState: responsibility is knowing one color and its single successor. Attributes: none (stateless). Methods: getColor(), next().
FixedTimingStrategy: responsibility is returning a pre-configured duration per color. Attributes: durations map. Methods: getDurationSeconds(color).
PedestrianSignal: responsibility is reacting to a vehicle signal change by updating a WALK/DON’T WALK indicator. Attributes: crossingId. Methods: onSignalChange(signalId, newColor).

metadata.alt: Three interfaces, SignalTimingStrategy, SignalObserver and SignalState, each with their concrete implementations

blocks.text: Each interface exists to isolate one specific axis of change. SignalTimingStrategy isolates timing rules, SignalObserver isolates reactions to change, and SignalState isolates the color transition rules themselves. A new requirement almost always maps to a new implementation of exactly one of these three interfaces, rather than a change to existing, already-tested code.
Three workflows matter most for this system: the routine phase cycle, an emergency vehicle override, and a pedestrian crossing request.

metadata.alt: The controller forcing the North-South signal green and the East-West signal red, each notifying its pedestrian signal

blocks.text: This is the routine, repeating heartbeat of the entire system, the controller sets one signal green and its perpendicular counterpart red, waits out the configured duration, then begins the transition toward the opposite pairing.

metadata.alt: An emergency dispatcher requesting priority clearance, forcing one direction green and holding it until released

blocks.text: An emergency override bypasses the normal phase timer entirely, forcing the requested direction green and its perpendicular counterpart red immediately, then resuming the normal cycle once released.

metadata.alt: A pedestrian pressing a crossing button, the controller waiting for a safe phase boundary before granting an early WALK signal

blocks.text: A pedestrian request is never granted instantly, the controller waits for the next safe phase boundary (it never interrupts an in-progress green phase mid-way) before shortening the cycle to grant the crossing.

metadata.alt: The repeating loop: apply phase, notify observers, wait, advance, apply the next phase

items: Happy path: controller applies phase 0 (NS green, EW red), waits the configured duration, advances to phase 1 (NS yellow), then phase 2 (EW green, NS red), then phase 3 (EW yellow), then back to phase 0.

Failure scenario, missing timing config: if a timing strategy has no duration registered for a color, getDurationSeconds() throws immediately rather than silently returning a default that could be unsafe.

Failure scenario, observer throws: a broken observer should not be allowed to prevent the signal’s own state from updating correctly, observer notification failures should be isolated and logged, not allowed to propagate back into TrafficSignal.
TrafficSignal.advance(): moves the signal to its state’s next() color and notifies observers.
TrafficSignal.forceState(SignalState): immediately sets a specific state, used by both the controller’s phase cycle and emergency overrides.
TrafficSignal.getCurrentColor() / getCurrentDurationSeconds(): read-only accessors for the signal’s current status.
IntersectionController.step(): advances the intersection to its next safe phase.
SignalTimingStrategy.getDurationSeconds(SignalColor): the single method every timing strategy must implement.

metadata.alt: Requesting a duration for an unconfigured color throws rather than silently defaulting

items: Invalid input: constructing an IntersectionController with two null signals should fail fast with a clear error, an intersection cannot exist without both signals.

Resource unavailable: a timing strategy with a missing color mapping throws an IllegalStateException (Java) / ValueError (Python) / runtime_error (C++) rather than defaulting to an arbitrary duration.
Business-rule violation: any attempted external call that would set both perpendicular signals green must be rejected at the controller level, never exposed as a possible state at all.
System failure: if the scheduler thread crashes mid-cycle, the last applied phase must remain in effect (fail safe), not revert to an undefined or all-green state.

metadata.alt: A scheduler thread and an emergency override thread both needing to safely mutate the same shared signal state

blocks.text: The scheduler thread calling step() on a timer, and an emergency dispatcher thread calling forceState() at an arbitrary moment, both touch the same TrafficSignal state. Both paths must be synchronized around the same lock so a scheduler-driven transition and an emergency override can never interleave into an invalid intermediate state (for example, one thread reading a stale color while another is mid-update). In Java, this means synchronizing advance()/forceState() on the TrafficSignal instance itself; in Python, a threading.Lock guarding the same two methods; in C++, a std::mutex serving the same purpose.

items: Adding a new timing strategy (e.g. SensorAdaptiveTimingStrategy that shortens green when no cross-traffic is detected) requires only a new class implementing SignalTimingStrategy, zero changes to TrafficSignal or IntersectionController.
Adding a new observer type (e.g. a ConnectedVehicleNotifier broadcasting signal changes to nearby cars) requires only a new SignalObserver implementation.

Supporting a third perpendicular direction (a five-way intersection) would require generalizing IntersectionController’s fixed NS/EW fields into a list of signal groups with a more general phase table, a larger but still localized change.
Future work: coordinating multiple adjacent intersections for a "green wave" would sit as a new layer above IntersectionController, not a modification to it.
Single Responsibility: TrafficSignal only manages one signal’s state and notifications, IntersectionController only coordinates phase timing, timing logic lives entirely in SignalTimingStrategy.
Open/Closed: new states, timing strategies, and observers can all be added without modifying existing classes.
Liskov Substitution: any SignalTimingStrategy implementation can replace another without breaking TrafficSignal, since all it relies on is getDurationSeconds().
Interface Segregation: SignalState, SignalTimingStrategy and SignalObserver are each a single narrow method, no implementation is forced to support behavior it does not need.
Dependency Inversion: TrafficSignal depends on the SignalTimingStrategy and SignalObserver interfaces, never on concrete implementations directly.
System startup: both signals must initialize into a safe state (one green, one red) before any external caller can interact with them, never both red-then-uninitialized.
Simultaneous pedestrian requests from both crossings: only one can be granted an early transition per cycle, the second must wait for the following cycle.

Emergency override requested while a pedestrian crossing is already in progress: the emergency clearance takes priority, but the pedestrian signal must still be safely set to DON’T WALK before the conflicting direction goes green.
Timing strategy returning a zero or negative duration: should be rejected at configuration time, not discovered mid-cycle.
advance() / forceState(): O(k) where k is the number of registered observers for that signal, dominated by the observer notification loop.
step(): O(1) phase lookup plus the cost of the two forceState() calls it makes.
getDurationSeconds(): O(1) for FixedTimingStrategy’s map lookup.
Space: O(n) for n registered observers per signal, plus O(1) fixed state per signal and per controller.

metadata.alt: INTERSECTION containing TRAFFIC_SIGNAL rows, each with a SIGNAL_STATE_LOG history and a linked TIMING_STRATEGY configuration

blocks.text: Even though the live control loop runs in memory, an audit trail and configuration store are still valuable in production. INTERSECTION holds one row per physical intersection, TRAFFIC_SIGNAL one row per direction within it, SIGNAL_STATE_LOG records every color change for auditing and analytics, and TIMING_STRATEGY stores the configured durations so they can be tuned without a code deployment.

items: How would you extend this design to coordinate a "green wave" across multiple adjacent intersections?
How would you incorporate live sensor data (e.g. induction loops detecting waiting vehicles) into the timing strategy safely?
How would you test that the safety invariant (never both directions green) can never be violated, even under concurrent access?
How would this design change if the intersection needed to support a dedicated left-turn arrow phase?

blocks.text: SignalColor.java / signal_color.py / signal_color part of the C++ header:

codes.python:
from enum import Enum


class SignalColor(Enum):
    RED = "RED"
    YELLOW = "YELLOW"
    GREEN = "GREEN"

blocks.text: Complete, self-contained, directly runnable file (every class above combined into one file per language, exactly as you would actually copy, compile and run it):

items: Why is the phase modeled as a single integer (0-3) inside IntersectionController rather than letting each signal decide its own next color independently? Because independent decisions could momentarily both be green, the controller must own the joint invariant, not each signal separately.

Why does forceState() exist separately from advance()? advance() always follows the State pattern’s natural next(), forceState() is needed for phase resets and emergency overrides, which must be able to jump to any state, not just the next one in sequence.

Why is PedestrianSignal an observer rather than something IntersectionController calls directly? Because the controller should not need to know pedestrian signals exist at all, that responsibility belongs entirely to TrafficSignal’s own observer list.

An alternative design could store phase transitions as data (a table of phase-to-signal-state mappings) rather than a switch statement, more flexible for many signal groups, but harder to read for the simple two-direction case this problem targets.

A simpler design could skip the State pattern entirely and just store a SignalColor enum with a helper function computing the next color, fewer classes, but transition logic and color both live in one place, making it harder to extend with, say, a flashing-amber maintenance state later.

Using a full event bus instead of a direct observer list would decouple observers even further, at the cost of added infrastructure complexity that is not justified at the scale of a single intersection.
Log every state transition (already modeled via SIGNAL_STATE_LOG) so unsafe states can be reconstructed and audited after the fact.
Add a watchdog that forces a flashing-red failsafe state if the scheduler thread stops advancing phases unexpectedly, rather than freezing on the last active color indefinitely.
Expose timing configuration through a separate configuration service so traffic engineers can tune durations without redeploying code.
Add metrics (phase duration actually observed vs configured) to detect drift caused by system load or scheduling delays.
